newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Producers try to boost aluminium price.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Producers try to boost aluminium price.

text.p: Two major U.S. producers attempted to give flagging aluminium prices a boost and one called for an inquiry by the London Metal Exchange into ways to prevent price manipulation.
Among other commodities grain markets in Chicago surged higher in response to dry weather in the U.S. Midwest and gold continued its slow recovery from recent 12 year lows.
Alcoa and Reynolds Metals, two of the world's biggest aluminium producers both firmly re-stated that they would not be starting-up their idled smelter capacity until the market needs it.
"We have no intention to restart that capacity in the short term," Reynolds chairman and CEO Jeremiah Sheehan said.
Aluminium on the London Metal Exchange (LME) rose $18 during Friday's trading to edge back above $1,600 but was still well below this year's early March high around $1,700 a tonne.
This was a bone of contention for Alcoa chief executive Paul O'Neill who said that LME inventories were shrinking by the day but the price was going down, in defiance of basic textbook economics.
"That suggests something, perhaps including intentional manipulation," O'Neill said, adding that he intended to write to the LME.
LME warehouse stocks have been declining steadily this year and currently stand at 654,375 tonnes against 955,850 tonnes at the start of 1997.
In Chicago fears that forecast rainfall would miss some of the dry corn growing areas of the U.S. lifted corn prices in the grain pit, and soyabeans too.

This dry weather threat to the potential yield of both crops saw corn prices up around six cents a bushel a midday at around $2.53 for September futures and soyabeans up 12 cents with September at $6.56 a bushel.
Gold's performance provided a crumb of comfort for the few remaining bulls in the market with a close above $324.00 an ounce showing a gain of nearly five dollars since Thursday.

But most traders still reckoned this bounce, from 12 year lows of around $314 last week, was nothing more than an overdue correction to a market that had become very much oversold on the way down to those lows.
